extracted.intended_audience: journalism students, reporters, editors, and newsroom managers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on how news organizations (magazines and TV networks) select, edit, prioritize, and assemble stories under deadline pressure, including organizational roles, delegation, autonomy, morale, and final-stage production practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respect and evaluate superiors' suggestions
rubrics_metrics.description: Pay close attention to the suggestions from superiors because they may be intended to set a precedent, but such suggestions can be questioned within limits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat upward suggestions as potentially precedent-setting; defer when appropriate but recognize that top editors/producers' power is not absolute and may be negotiated or questioned tactfully. Example anti-pattern: ignoring a superior's suggested angle because it 'feels wrong'—this risks creating a precedent gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate delegation by top editors/producers
rubrics_metrics.description: Top editors and producers cannot do everything and must delegate story selection and editing decisions to assistants and section heads; the extent of delegation depends on organizational tradition and personal style.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design delegation to balance centralized control and section autonomy. Monitor delegation effects (e.g., autonomous 'feudal baronies' vs. centralized editing). Change delegation only if it will improve quality or morale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protect individual autonomy of journalists
rubrics_metrics.description: Journalists claim freedom from interference and the right to make their own news judgments; autonomy in production is a function of seniority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Allow reporters and writers to select facts, draw conclusions, and form evaluations; treat autonomy as valuable but uncertain—senior staff have more leeway. Anti-pattern: micromanaging novice and senior writers alike.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senior editor control over story length
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior editors generally decide how many words a story 'deserves,' although writers may later choose to exceed the prescribed length; a writer's judgment is sustained if the story is good enough.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate word counts with senior editors; ensure the argument for extra length is based on substance and quality. Scoring note: exceptional stories can override length constraints.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors' role in organization and leads, limited substantive alteration
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior editors typically offer suggestions about story organization and possible leads; they seldom suggest different conclusions or evaluations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect and accept stylistic and organizational edits more than substantive rewrites. If a senior editor proposes substantive changes, prepare evidence and clear writing to defend your position. Anti-pattern: presenting disagreements as purely personal rather than factual.

rubrics_metrics.name: Top-editor final authority and indirect influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Top editors have the last word: they can order rewrites, kill pieces, or indirectly nudge a point of view (e.g., by asking for new versions or giving the piece to someone else).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manage relationships with top editors, anticipate indirect signals (requests for new versions), and craft rewrites that preserve your core reporting while satisfying editorial concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Edit to manage audience reaction
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors may 'soften' a harsh judgment or edit out a conclusion that could result in angry letters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance truthful reporting with awareness of likely audience responses; use editing to reduce unnecessary provocation without undermining factual integrity. Example: tone down speculative language that could be misread as accusation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Medium-specific autonomy and constraints
rubrics_metrics.description: Television reporters have greater autonomy in production because they film far from headquarters, but television offers fewer opportunities for evaluative text and producers intervene more on controversial stories or under time pressure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt reporting and editing practices to medium: in TV prioritize clarity and usable footage; in print prioritize evaluative context and space for conclusions. Anti-pattern: applying print-level evaluative expectations to short TV items.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain staff morale to preserve quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Top editors and producers must uphold staff morale—through ambience, working conditions, and treatment of staff—because low morale reduces journalists' willingness to exert extra effort for informational and stylistic originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use managerial actions (fair assignments, reasonable edits, explanations for kills) to sustain morale. Monitor morale indicators (griping, turnover, productivity) and address bureaucratic frustrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use editorial scheduling to preserve morale
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors avoid killing a section more than three or four times consecutively, assign at least one cover story to every section each year, and ensure bureaus see their efforts in print or on air regularly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan rotations and guarantees for sections/bureaus to avoid repeated exclusion. Use diplomatic story placement to reward contributors. Anti-pattern: repeatedly removing the same section without explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Respond to staff grievances and pace reforms cautiously
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers' protests (e.g., for more time, longer stories, less heavy editing) have produced reforms, but editors caution against unduly rapid change; reforms may take years and be incremental.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat staff complaints as signals for structural adjustments, but balance reforms with institutional stability and production constraints. Example: gradually increase permitted lengths where feasible rather than sudden wholesale change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider labor market and staffing dynamics
rubrics_metrics.description: The bargaining power of writers and researchers depends on labor market conditions; recruitment, promotion, and inclusion (e.g., hiring women, promoting researchers to reporters) affect organizational dynamics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor external labor market tightness into retention, promotion, and assignment policies. Use hiring and training paths to address shortages and improve diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply seniority but reward merit and scoops
rubrics_metrics.description: Seniority principles assign safer stories to veterans and more marginal pieces to younger staff, but upward mobility is often driven by merit (scoops, strong reporting) even if organizational politics and background matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance predictable seniority-based assignments with opportunities for merit-driven advancement. Encourage young reporters to seek high-impact assignments when feasible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize ratings and audience performance in internal politics
rubrics_metrics.description: Factions and power struggles in news organizations are often won by those who deliver rating successes; executives with low ratings are replaced despite internal alliances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make editorial decisions mindful of audience impact and ratings; organizational survival may hinge on measurable audience success. Anti-pattern: prioritizing internal politics over demonstrated audience outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Structure production around deadlines (assembly-line/funnel)
rubrics_metrics.description: Deadlines determine divisions of labor and routinize selection/production: initial long story lists are winnowed (funnel/accordion model), lists are padded with postponable items and evergreens, and breaking stories have first priority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain padded lists (postponable items, pegless 'evergreens') to allow last-minute breaking stories; implement a clear winnowing schedule tied to deadlines. Example: prepare timeless features to fill space if needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement prekilling to manage space and workload
rubrics_metrics.description: Some back-of-the-book sections are 'prekilled' at the start of selection to focus resources; top editors won't kill a section repeatedly to protect morale.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use prekilling strategically to limit wasted effort on stories unlikely to run; communicate prekilling decisions to affected staff and rotate to minimize morale problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose cover stories for perceived importance and strategic competition
rubrics_metrics.description: The cover subject is deemed the most important story (usually 5–6 pages); weekly cover conferences enable long-range planning, but the top editor makes the final cover choice, which confers prestige and signals importance to readers and peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select covers based on newsworthiness, reader interest, and strategic competition with rivals; expect final decisions to be revisited late in the production cycle and to change for breaking stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coordinate visual/printing constraints in planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Color pages are limited to specific spreads and go to press earlier than black-and-white pages, requiring advance planning and alignment of sections using color.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan color photo placement ahead of deadline and align sections across required spreads; be aware production timing differences for color vs. black-and-white when scheduling stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fit TV stories to segment formats and available minutes
rubrics_metrics.description: Producers must assemble film and tell stories to fit the available 22–23 minutes of news, dividing programs into segments (e.g., five segments at CBS, four at NBC) that shape story length and selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select and edit TV stories to match network segment structures and minute budgets; when format changes (e.g., segment count) occur, adjust story selection strategy accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enable rapid last-stage decision-making and revisions
rubrics_metrics.description: In the final hours (TV's last 90 minutes; magazines' Days 4–5), lineups are revised, stories are trimmed or substituted, and producers/editors make rapid phone calls and edits up to air/press time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain clear communication channels, quick review protocols, and the ability to make fast technical and editorial edits (e.g., cut 15 seconds of film). Expect lineup changes as late as just before air or press run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Organize magazine stories for logical flow, concision, and iterative editing
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers must assemble information from files around a framework that flows logically, with the fewest words, minimal repetition, and few unnecessary bridges; senior editors and top editors iteratively edit, with cover stories possibly rewritten several times.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritize strong organization and concise prose in drafts; anticipate multiple rounds of editorial revision, especially for cover pieces. Anti-pattern: producing verbose copy that requires heavy late-stage cuts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage page allocations and front-of-book prioritization
rubrics_metrics.description: Senior editors plan section makeup and page requirements; front-of-the-book sections can usually secure more pages and are prioritized as events flow, while back sections may be cut or killed to make space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiate page needs early; be prepared for appeals to top editors if additional pages are required. Anticipate that front-of-book stories will have preferential space during updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use 'timeless features' (evergreens) to add scheduling flexibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The list includes 'timeless features' or 'pegless wonders' which are not pegged to events and can be run any time to fill space.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain a stock of evergreen pieces to deploy when breaking news displaces pegged content or when unexpected space opens. Keep evergreens updated so they remain publishable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize breaking news and critically assess anticipated events
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking stories (unexpected events like deaths, disasters, indictments) have first priority; anticipated events may be dropped if they repeat earlier coverage or fail to yield new material.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Always assess anticipated events for newness; hold back expendable pieces in padded lists and be ready to 'stop the presses' for major breaking items. Anti-pattern: rigidly sticking to planned items despite major breaking developments.
